summary:
Selangor stands under Malaysia's national framework: the federal Penal Code, the national rules on identity documents and the entry provisions recorded in Malaysia's own dossier apply to visitors here as elsewhere in the country. Two further layers operate inside the state. The Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 binds Muslims, and Selangor's Islamic religious department polices appearance and public conduct under it.

In February 2021 the Federal Court struck down provisions of the Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 as exceeding the state's legislative power. The ruling turned on state legislative competence and did not decriminalise the conduct under federal law, so the exposure a visitor faces in Selangor did not end with it.

Selangor's enactment bars Muslim men from dressing as women, and the state's religious officers enforce it with no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dress. A Muslim trans woman in the state is therefore exposed to arrest on an undefined standard judged by religious officials rather than by any written test.

The most prominent state action in this record is the 2021 prosecution of Nur Sajat, a transgender woman and cosmetics entrepreneur. She failed to appear in a Selangor court to answer charges of "insulting Islam" brought over her attire; the state's religious department issued a warrant for her arrest and announced that it had mobilised 122 religious-affairs officers to hunt her down, then sought her extradition from Thailand. She was permitted to remain under UNHCR protection and later settled in Australia. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters cite the deployment as evidence of how far authorities will go to enforce rigid gender norms.

Selangor's Sharia court has also sentenced five men to six to seven months' imprisonment with six strokes of the cane for same-sex conduct, a custodial and corporal outcome that shows the state's religious courts remain an active route of punishment rather than a dormant one.
tangentialFactors:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile, last updated 16 December 2025, places Selangor's enforcement inside a nationwide crackdown on LGBT people that it dates from the 2018 general election. The same profile records that by June 2021 at least 1,733 people had attended state "rehabilitation programmes"; that figure is national, not Selangor-specific, and no state-by-state breakdown is given.

The August 2022 report by Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters drew on investigations covering seven jurisdictions at once: Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah. Selangor is therefore one of several states where the same pattern of state-backed discrimination was documented, not an isolated case. That report found state "rehabilitation" programmes internalise discrimination and foment self-hatred among participants.
localsOnly:
Selangor's own sharia provisions reach residents directly and in ways that do not apply to non-Muslims. Under section 54 of the state enactment, a Sharia court may commit a woman convicted of musahaqah to an approved home for up to six months, an involuntary confinement ordered on the basis of her conduct rather than any criminal sentence.

Residents who are Muslim are bound by the cross-dressing prohibition and by the state religious department's enforcement of it, and the absence of a legal definition of transgender dress leaves the standard entirely in the hands of the officers applying it. Muslim residents also face the state's "rehabilitation" programmes, which the Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters investigation found operate to internalise discrimination.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sentencing of the five men by the Selangor Sharia court is recorded without a date; only the profile carrying it, last updated 16 December 2025, is dated. When the sentence was passed is unresolved in this record.

Whether the provisions of the Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 struck down in February 2021 have been re-enacted, replaced or left dormant is not sourced here.

The 1,733 figure for attendance at state "rehabilitation programmes" is a national total as of June 2021. No Selangor-specific count of participants is available in this inventory, and the state's own share of that total is unresolved.

This record's inventory contains no Selangor-specific incident of violence against trans people, and no Selangor-specific data on identity-document processing, entry screening or facility access. Those layers are governed by the national record and are not sourced at state level here.
